projects.title: 3D Agentic Evacuation Simulation
projects.summary: Browser 3-D evacuation twins of Mariupol, Lower Manhattan, the Las Vegas Strip and Miami in which a synthetic population of households chooses between real road-routed exits, for planning and teaching.

contribution.roleNote: Joins the ETC mariupol-evacuation-model data with the agent model of Google Cloud Platform's Race Condition, via the ETC fork race-condition-mod.

narrative.problem: An evacuation is many people, imperfect information, shared routes, bottlenecks and a clock. A census records who people are, but not who they travel with or how they behave, and those are what decide who is still inside when a route closes.
narrative.decision: Renders deck.gl layers over a keyless CARTO basemap with open Sentinel-2 imagery and OpenStreetMap building centroids, instead of the photogrammetry model and bespoke Three.js scene of the Race Condition fork it builds on.
narrative.tradeoff: Buildings are extruded columns whose heights exist only where OpenStreetMap records them (96% in Lower Manhattan, 0% in Mariupol), and the 10 m Sentinel-2 mosaic softens when zoomed to a street.
narrative.limitation: Zone populations are modelled and county cohort figures are applied to districts; household-unit and behaviour mixes, transit boarding capacities and weather multipliers are modelled, not sourced; transit covers Lower Manhattan only.
narrative.caveat: Open-data and non-operational: a planning and teaching artifact. No agent corresponds to a real person, and nothing here is operational guidance or an evacuation plan for any of these cities.

projects.title: After the Corridor
projects.summary: A research report for funders and humanitarian researchers that reads the CoLab's evacuation prototypes and forced-labour risk index together and extends them to refugee economic inclusion at Dzaleka, Malawi.

contribution.roleNote: Ethical Tech CoLab research report; the published report lists Prof. Yorke E. Rhodes III and Sylvia Maier as faculty directors.

narrative.problem: A successful evacuation typically ends in a camp and years of protracted displacement. At Dzaleka Refugee Camp, Malawi, humanitarian financing has collapsed while an encampment policy bars residents from working, and the camp now holds 53,000 to 60,000 people in a site built for 10,000 to 12,000.
narrative.decision: Names the one thing the lab refuses to build, biometric identity for displaced people, and records that refusal as a versioned decision pattern (DDC-0001) rather than leaving it implicit.
narrative.tradeoff: Services that depend on verified individual identity are ruled out, so the proposed infrastructure has to rely on measurement, aggregate evidence, privacy-preserving rails and rights information instead.
narrative.limitation: Maturity varies by tool: only the ERCF cost engine is validated, and for evacuation; the livelihoods index and inclusion simulator are proposed, and their weights and thresholds stay provisional until expert-elicited and calibrated.
narrative.caveat: Views and findings are the researchers' own, not those of NYU, Microsoft, UNHCR, WFP or any partner institution; external programs cited are evidence, not CoLab partnerships.

projects.title: Agentic Behavior Observatory
projects.summary: A browser and command-line tool that scores GitHub repositories on six axes of agentic-behavior modeling, with file-and-line evidence, for researchers reviewing synthetic-population work.

narrative.problem: When someone builds a system that generates or evaluates synthetic populations at scale, it is hard to see what they are actually modeling and what they leave out: which demographic dimensions appear, which model versions the results rest on, and whether one agent's private context is kept from another's.
narrative.decision: Scores every repository by signal coverage against one taxonomy file (analyzer/signals.py) that is exported to the browser, so the dashboard and the CLI score identically and each point links to the file and line where its signal fired.
narrative.tradeoff: Regular expressions match vocabulary, not meaning: a repository that discusses a technique without implementing it still fires the signal, and a score measures coverage of the taxonomy rather than scientific quality.
narrative.limitation: Up to 120 files per repository are read, so large repositories are sampled rather than read whole, and the demographic vocabulary is a fixed English list that under-reports populations described in other terms.
narrative.caveat: Scores are signal coverage against the taxonomy, not a quality judgment; a low context-isolation score marks a boundary nobody wrote down, not proof of a leak.

projects.title: Agentic Language Development
projects.summary: A research concept and preregistrable study protocol asking whether two isolated artificial agents can invent a grounded, auditable language through shared experience.

narrative.problem: Studying whether two agents can establish stable meanings without a supplied dictionary requires telling genuine, causally used communication apart from a memorized lookup code. Pretrained language models already contain human-language concepts, so restricting their external channel does not make them language-naive.
narrative.decision: Each agent (Baby A and Baby B) has its own DTSF digital twin, private memory and mandatory chronological language ledger kept with hash chains and signed Merkle checkpoints, and may communicate only through a controlled non-human Symbol Gateway, watched by a BabySitter that never teaches or translates.
narrative.tradeoff: Strict channel isolation and monitor-only supervision make any emergent language auditable, but they rule out teaching or reward shaping by the observer, and the ledger, channel and anchoring machinery has to be built and verified before any experiment can run.
narrative.limitation: The repository is in the foundation implementation phase: the workspace, runtime schemas, twin-pack skeletons, evidence schema and ledger validators exist, but independent ledger/channel hash chaining is still ahead and no experiment results are claimed.
narrative.caveat: Pre-results research concept: the site and page-turn manuscript describe a study protocol; no experiment results are claimed yet.

projects.title: Wayfinder — Agentic Ontology
projects.summary: A concept for a personal AI agent that acts for its person from a small, typed ontology and writes every step to a personal ledger the person can inspect.

narrative.problem: A personal AI agent that acts for someone can believe, share and do things its person cannot see afterwards. Wayfinder aims to let the person see what the agent believed, what it shared, what it did and why.
narrative.decision: Wayfinder is designed to run on TrustGraph, the open-source ontology runtime for AI agents, unmodified and as deployed containers; each job of the ontology is built on an existing TrustGraph feature and the repository contains no TrustGraph code.
narrative.tradeoff: Relying on TrustGraph as an unmodified dependency, pinned to release v2.11, keeps the project small but ties its capabilities and upgrade path to what TrustGraph already offers.
narrative.limitation: The README states the status as "concept and plan approved; building milestone M1. Nothing runnable yet." The site's simulation dashboard and two-sides screen are synthetic and deterministic illustrations of the design.
narrative.caveat: The simulations are synthetic and deterministic: scripted flows with template text, no LLM runs and no real data. Only the lease negotiation is computed live, by the vendored Neocloud engine.

projects.title: AI's Carbon Footprint
projects.summary: An Ethical Tech CoLab academic report for non-technical readers on the environmental impact of AI: energy use in training and inference, data-center and hardware toll, and mitigation and policy options.

contribution.roleNote: Advised by Professor Yorke Rhodes III and written by eight Ethical Tech CoLab researchers, per the README.

narrative.problem: AI's rapid expansion carries a significant but often overlooked environmental cost, from the energy demands of training and inference to the toll of data centers and hardware, and the policy debate needs those costs stated clearly.
narrative.decision: The report was put through an independent academic peer review, and the review, its 'major revisions' verdict and each revision applied are published alongside the report rather than replaced silently.
narrative.tradeoff: Unresolved criticism stays visible: the review's objection that the thesis qualifier 'without hindering its development' is asserted and never argued is still marked open.
narrative.limitation: The thesis that mitigation need not hinder AI's development remains unargued, and the rebound effect of efficiency gains is not engaged; inference-energy scenarios are illustrative upper bounds.
narrative.caveat: Inference-energy figures are illustrative projections and upper bounds. Views are the researchers' own, not the official positions of NYU, Microsoft or any partner institution.

projects.title: AI Models Research
projects.summary: A research knowledge base for researchers, policy analysts and engineers comparing AI model families on capability, accuracy, speed, energy use and token cost, with every figure sourced, dated and graded.

contribution.roleNote: Ethical Tech CoLab research repository.

narrative.problem: Public discussion of model capability is dominated by provider launch materials and single-number leaderboard rankings, often produced under evaluation conditions that are undisclosed, unreproducible, or not comparable across providers, so it is hard to choose a model for a given task, budget and deployment constraint on evidence.
narrative.decision: Separates independently verified measurement (Grade A), institutional primary research (Grade B) and provider-reported claims (Grade C), and generates every comparison table from source-linked CSV records that validation scripts check.
narrative.tradeoff: Claims that cannot meet the standard are recorded as 'Not publicly disclosed' or 'Insufficient independent evidence' rather than estimated, so many cells stay empty and no model ranking is published.
narrative.limitation: Research cut-off 2026-07-22. Phase 1 is complete; chapters, data and navigation are partial; the sixteen model-family profiles are not started; energy, latency and factuality datasets are empty; and the survey is not peer reviewed.
narrative.caveat: Prices, rankings and availability are historical records as of the cut-off date, not current facts; nothing here is legal, financial or procurement advice.

projects.title: AI-Powered Assistance in Formulating Research Questions
projects.summary: A plain-language paper, reusable prompt and journal-credibility rubric on how AI can help researchers form answerable research questions, and the guardrails that use requires.

contribution.roleNote: Masters research by an Ethical Tech CoLab student cohort at the NYU Center for Global Affairs; Yorke is listed among the authors.

narrative.problem: AI is increasingly used to help academic researchers pose research questions by mining large literatures, but the same tools can hallucinate citations, fabricate conceptual linkages, overstate consensus and shift a researcher's framing toward what the model predicts rather than what the literature supports.
narrative.decision: Pairs AI for ideation with AI for critical interrogation: a reusable researcher prompt that scores sources against a fixed journal-credibility rubric, plus a proposed red-team agent that audits citations and flags unsupported claims.
narrative.tradeoff: The guidance is model-agnostic text rather than software, so nothing enforces it: its value depends on researchers independently checking sources, and the red-team agent remains a proposal.
narrative.limitation: The prompt is unevaluated. Peer review recommended major revisions and found every effect claim is design argument; a minimal evaluation protocol is sketched but has not been run, and the planned Next.js application is not built.
narrative.caveat: The paper was partly generated and checked with the M365 Copilot Researcher Agent running OpenAI GPT v5; treat AI-suggested research questions as exploratory starting points, not conclusions.

projects.title: The 37-Second Blind Spot: A Million Green Tests, One Missing Assumption
projects.summary: A reproducible Ariane 501 study that uses seeded Monte Carlo experiments to show what must be true for testing or AI evaluations to uncover a failure, for people who design evaluations.

contribution.roleNote: Independent analysis inspired by Channi Greenwall's article on Ariane 501; no affiliation with the author, ESA, CNES or NIST.

narrative.problem: Large counts of passing tests can create false confidence. The Ariane 501 failure was testable and preventable, yet a million tests drawn from the wrong input distribution, run against an idealized stub or judged by a weak oracle, can all pass. Evaluators of AI and software systems need to know what conditions a test world must meet before more tests help.
narrative.decision: Runs 1,600,000 seeded synthetic test opportunities, signed-conversion boundary tests, barrier ablations and a 128-configuration prerequisite experiment in a standard-library Python model, with a --check mode that reruns every experiment and compares eight generated artifacts byte-for-byte.
narrative.tradeoff: Fixed seeds and a dependency-free toy model make every count reproducible offline with no API key, but the model relies on invented, labeled values and distributions instead of the original flight executable, a calibrated BH transfer function or raw telemetry.
narrative.limitation: It is a retrospective toy model, not recovered Ada source, a digital twin or flight certification, and not proof that an AI system would have found the problem without hindsight. Evidence retention and enforced response are modeled, not measured human outcomes.
narrative.caveat: All inputs are synthetic and labeled: results are not measured Ariane 4/Ariane 5 trajectories or estimated launch failure rates, and the modeled remedies are illustrative, not engineering guidance.

projects.title: Digital Provenance Passport
projects.summary: A research prototype agent that traces the provenance of artworks and artifacts, flags looting and repatriation risk, and issues a signed, tamper-evident passport for each object.

contribution.roleNote: Masters research at the NYU Center for Global Affairs under the Ethical Tech CoLab, built for the Microsoft × Coinbase x402 hackathon.

narrative.problem: Provenance for many objects is incomplete or contested, and the registers that certify stolen cultural property have no public API. Material taken from archaeological sites or under colonial rule was never reported stolen, so it cannot appear in a stolen-property register at all.
narrative.decision: Grounding searches an allowlist of authoritative sources and extracts only cited facts, so a claim with no source is never produced; no register check can return "clear", and every check, including failed ones, is signed into the Passport with its caveat.
narrative.tradeoff: The sourcing rule blocks unsourced claims, not false ones, and the allowlist of mostly Western institutions searches best where objects are already well documented and worst for source-country, colonial-era and archaeological material.
narrative.limitation: None of the fifteen catalogue scores was computed by the pipeline; each was assigned by hand. The web pipeline and the canonical scorer still return different numbers, and the national heritage authorities of source countries are not covered.
narrative.caveat: A research prototype for academic demonstration: outputs are indicative, not a determination of title. The published site is a pre-rendered capture whose passports are signed with a throwaway key; payments use the Base Sepolia testnet.

projects.title: Avatar Impact Stories — Many Voices
projects.summary: An interactive kiosk wall that plays first-person survivor testimonies through AI-generated avatars, so accounts of trafficking and forced labour can be shown while survivors' identities stay protected.

contribution.roleNote: Fall 2025 Generative AI for Good cohort project: students made the avatar stories, advised by Shiran Mlamdovsky Somech; Yorke maintains the kiosk.

narrative.problem: Survivor testimony is the most persuasive evidence there is and the most dangerous thing a survivor can give: a real face beside an account of trafficking or forced labour can expose someone to retaliation, while silhouettes, voice modulation or actors cost what makes testimony land.
narrative.decision: Each account is delivered by a synthetic D-ID presenter, with an AI watermark over every playing video, so the testimony stays first-person while the identity behind it stays protected.
narrative.tradeoff: The presenters carry the limits of Fall 2025 tooling (lip-sync drift, fixed gaze, narrow emotional range), and testimony has to be cut to an avatar's short attention window of roughly 40 seconds to 2 minutes.
narrative.limitation: The avatars are a deliberately unrefreshed snapshot of Fall 2025 D-ID output, and the README reports no evaluation of how visitors respond to the wall.
narrative.caveat: Every presenter is synthetic; the accounts are not. They describe trafficking, forced and child labour, violence and conscription, presented plainly — please take care.

projects.title: Bare Metal Jacket
projects.summary: A self-hosted developer platform design that brings managed-PaaS deployment workflows, from Git push to a healthy HTTPS service, to organization-controlled bare-metal servers.

narrative.problem: Developers want to connect a Git repository, pick a branch and configuration, and receive a running HTTPS service without operating the underlying infrastructure by hand, while keeping operational control, portable OCI artifacts, transparent costs and repeatable recovery on hardware they own.
narrative.decision: The first implementation is deliberately Docker-native, bare-metal-first and single-node, validating the complete deployment path before introducing a distributed scheduler or Kubernetes.
narrative.tradeoff: Public or hostile multi-tenancy, autoscaling, multiple regions, GPU scheduling, managed databases and Kubernetes are explicitly deferred, so the first release serves trusted internal users on one server.
narrative.limitation: The repository is in Phase 0 (product, contract and threat definition): it has architecture, an API contract, a security model, local infrastructure composition and a sample workload, but no production control plane yet, and no license has been selected.
narrative.caveat: Phase 0 project: the site presents architecture, research and roadmap; the first release must not be treated as safe for hostile public multi-tenancy.

projects.title: Brooklyn Bridge Digital Twin
projects.summary: A browser-viewable 3D control model of the Brooklyn Bridge in which every dimension traces to a registered source with a confidence grade, for review and HO-scale model study.

narrative.problem: 3D models of landmark structures rarely show which dimensions were read from a source and which were guessed. The Brooklyn Bridge is well documented in the national record, yet turning HAER drawings, Washington Roebling's reports and NYC DOT studies into geometry still leaves gaps that are easy to hide.
narrative.decision: Grades every control dimension against a registered source and lets viewers untick INFERRED and ASSUMED geometry; anything unsourced is graded D, drawn with a dotted outline and linked to a named open question.
narrative.tradeoff: The honest view is sparse: with inferred and assumed parts hidden, only the two anchorages and seven station markers remain, and photographs may inform material or arrangement but can never set a dimension.
narrative.limitation: At Milestone 1, 14 of 101 controls are placeholders, the approach supports are drawn as the wrong kind of structure, the tower taper is invented, and four of nine registered source conflicts remain open.
narrative.caveat: Not an as-built survey: much of the geometry is inferred or assumed, and known errors are registered rather than hidden. Untick INFERRED and ASSUMED in the viewer to see what the sources actually locate.

projects.title: CERAI — Civilian Evacuation Risk Anticipation Index
projects.summary: A research prototype that scores civilian risk during evacuations in armed conflict, with Monte Carlo sensitivity analysis, to support International Humanitarian Law review and humanitarian planning.

contribution.roleNote: Developed by Teresa Cantero as part of PhD research at NYU School of Law on IHL and AI.

narrative.problem: Evacuation decisions in armed conflict must weigh hazards, infrastructure, population vulnerability, the information environment and weather against International Humanitarian Law obligations, and that reasoning is often hard for humanitarian and legal audiences such as the UN and ICRC to trace or audit.
narrative.decision: Combines multi-category risk indicators into a composite index with Monte Carlo sensitivity analysis and source-credibility tagging, and keeps endangerment separate from feasibility so operational difficulty cannot silently override the duty to protect, all in a single-file HTML prototype.
narrative.tradeoff: A single composite gauge makes risk legible and easy to audit in a browser, but it rests on a fixed weight vector and a 75% threshold that peer review flagged as false precision, and its Monte Carlo varies inputs rather than weights.
narrative.limitation: Peer review recommended major revisions; literature positioning beyond INFORM Severity and external data licensing remain open, the 75% threshold is only partially addressed, and evaluation is a retrospective face-validity table of four anchor cases.
narrative.caveat: Research prototype: outputs are indicative and not a substitute for operational decision-making or legal advice.

projects.title: Ethical Tech CoLab Board
projects.summary: A local-first spatial whiteboard for touch displays, classrooms, studios and workshops that runs in the browser and can replay how a session's ideas evolved.

narrative.problem: Classrooms, studios and workshops on touch displays need a shared thinking surface that runs without a server, keeps board content on the device, and can replay how ideas evolved.
narrative.decision: Live boards use a host-ordered star topology over encrypted WebRTC: edits to different objects merge in host order and, for the same object, the latest host-ordered change wins, intentionally avoiding CRDT and account/server complexity.
narrative.tradeoff: Concurrent changes to the same object are resolved by the last host-ordered edit rather than merged, and host traffic grows with both active artists and recipients, so the host needs a desktop or unmetered connection.
narrative.limitation: Seven participants are the validated working size; larger sessions should be benchmarked on their real network first. QR handoff and live boards depend on the public PeerJS signaling service, and VPNs or restrictive networks can block WebRTC.

projects.title: Commons Collective
projects.summary: An AI-assisted academic discussion draft, with a browser simulation lab, on collective bargaining institutions through which data contributors could share fairly in AI value, for researchers and funders.

contribution.roleNote: Developed from a session brief for the Ethical Tech CoLab.

narrative.problem: Institutions that let dispersed data creators, such as individual workers, platform users and small publishers, bargain collectively with AI labs are largely absent, and there is little agreement on what such an ecosystem would look like, how it should be governed or how it would pay.
narrative.decision: The Simulation Lab runs entirely on GitHub Pages in a Web Worker using the same versioned kernel as the Node tests, with no server, credentials, analytics or live AI calls; a run is replayed from its seed and configuration and checked against a state fingerprint.
narrative.tradeoff: With no live model calls, agent policies are scripted or seeded and the live P2 policy is unavailable in the static release, so results are conditional on stated assumptions rather than observed behaviour.
narrative.limitation: Not peer-reviewed and not a record of participant agreement; simulation inputs are illustrative and uncalibrated, and the funding trials are cohort-finance trials under explicit assumptions, not empirical observations.
narrative.caveat: Synthetic and uncalibrated: no real people, money or AI services are involved. People named in the report are a research circle, not authors or endorsers. Not legal or investment advice.

projects.title: CrowdDeck
projects.summary: An open-source venue runtime that runs a DJ deck engine and a TouchTunes-style crowd request jukebox on one scheduler, library and clock, for venues that are a jukebox by day and a DJ room by night.

narrative.problem: Every DJ application surveyed scores effectively zero on crowd participation, and every jukebox platform scores effectively zero on performance capability, yet real venues need both on a schedule. Existing open-source jukeboxes also depend on a host's consumer Spotify account, which conveys no public-performance rights.
narrative.decision: Writes the engine contract (CDEP, NDJSON over a local socket) first and keeps the planned GPL-2.0-or-later Mixxx engine behind a hard process boundary from the Apache-2.0 core, proven replaceable by a conformant stub engine and a browser Web Audio engine.
narrative.tradeoff: The project ships as two separate downloads and every engine call crosses an IPC boundary, so its latency budgets depend on measurements still outstanding; the split-licence position is accepted risk, with no legal review obtained or planned.
narrative.limitation: The build is in progress at 76 of 91 stories. The venue clients (patron, DJ console, display) still run on the silent stub engine, the native Mixxx engine is not built, and latency is measured only on WASAPI; other platforms need real audio and MIDI hardware.

projects.title: Digital 3D — Shared Contracts
projects.summary: Shared JSON schemas, a canonical coordinate frame and a framework-agnostic viewer kernel that let independently owned 3D modules, such as a bridge twin and a district twin, work together.

narrative.problem: Independently owned 3D modules, such as a bridge model and a neighbourhood model, must agree on where things are, which vertical datum is zero, how levels of detail relate and what one module may know about another; otherwise a bridge authored against mean high water can sit 0.59 m into buildings authored against NAVD88.
narrative.decision: The repository holds no module data, only normative JSON Schema 2020-12 contracts, a frozen canonical scene frame that modules copy byte-for-byte, and a framework-agnostic viewer kernel; every level of detail from every module is placed on one max_geometric_error_m axis.
narrative.tradeoff: Freezing the frame anchor and allowing only additions within a major version keeps every module's coordinates stable, but the anchor cannot be corrected for the life of contract version 1, and removing anything must wait for a new major version.
narrative.limitation: The bundled fixtures are tiny and synthetic and exist only to self-test the schemas; the contracts are consumed so far by two sibling modules, manhattan-bridge-3d and dumbo-district-3d, and the repository has no hosted demo of its own.

projects.title: Digital Passport for Artworks
projects.summary: A browser-based prototype for issuing, verifying and revoking digital passports for artworks, with duplicate detection and human review routing, all client-side.

contribution.roleNote: Originally by @ChristineLumen.

narrative.problem: An artwork's digital passport is only useful if the same work cannot be registered twice, even from a photo taken at a different angle, and if anyone can check that a passport was issued by a trusted authority and has not been altered or revoked.
narrative.decision: The whole lifecycle runs client-side in a single HTML file: fingerprints, similarity search, forgery-risk routing and a real ECDSA P-256 certificate chain via the Web Crypto API, with nothing leaving the browser tab except the optional MobileNet model.
narrative.tradeoff: With no server or database, there is no persistent registry: duplicate detection only compares submissions within one browser session, and refreshing the page clears all memory.
narrative.limitation: The README presents it as a prototype of the detection pipeline, not a production registry. The site notes that most forensic signals are hand-built heuristics kept as low-weight advisory signals, not a trained classifier.
narrative.caveat: Duplicate detection works within a single browser session only; refreshing the page clears all memory. Keys and certificates are generated in the browser for the demonstration.

projects.title: DPA — Digital Passport for Artworks
projects.summary: A working monorepo that consolidates five AABC × SDA Bocconi provenance prototypes into one pipeline that scores an artwork's provenance and issues one signed passport with role-based views.

contribution.roleNote: Consolidates five upstream prototypes; most package code was written by others and vendored (see ATTRIBUTION.md).

narrative.problem: An artwork whose provenance is uncertain is effectively invisible: it cannot be lent, studied, insured or claimed, because surfacing it exposes its holder to legal and reputational risk. narrative.limitation: Everything on the site runs on committed fixtures: no live register was contacted, notarisation runs in mock mode, demo signing keys are deterministic, Stage 0 capture is not yet wired into the pipeline, and two decisions are reopened.
narrative.caveat: Demonstration only: scores are computed over real cited sources, but no live register was queried and no attestation was written to any chain. The 3D exhibit object is procedural, not a scan of a real artefact.

projects.title: DropBoard
projects.summary: A shared drop-space in the browser where people in a meeting, or one person across devices, exchange files, links and text using a short access code, with no accounts or installs.

contribution.roleNote: Fork of alx-du/dropboard by Alex Du; the repository includes a build log and executive report written as a teaching deliverable on building with AI coding tools.

narrative.problem: Moving things between people mid-meeting is still awkward: links shared in a video call chat disappear when the call ends, teammates send files across several messaging apps, AirDrop only works Apple-to-Apple, and tools like Slack, Drive or Miro assume everyone shares a workspace and accounts.
narrative.decision: Boards are ephemeral sessions joined with a short human-readable access code and no user accounts; the deployed backend is Cloudflare Workers with Durable Objects for WebSocket sync and expiry, plus R2 for files, behind a backend-agnostic frontend switch.
narrative.tradeoff: Skipping accounts keeps a board usable within seconds on any device, but the access code becomes the only barrier, so it has to be treated like a meeting link rather than a password, and nothing is kept once a session expires.
narrative.limitation: It is a working demo under a working name: AI features are deferred, the Supabase backend is only a scaffolded alternative, and open questions remain about default expiry, sustainable file-size caps, host powers and abuse reporting.
narrative.caveat: Access codes are the only barrier to a board — treat them like a meeting link, not a password. Boards are ephemeral and their content is deleted when the session expires.

projects.title: ERCF — Evacuation Risk and Cost Framework
projects.summary: A decision-support tool for humanitarian planners that estimates the human and financial cost of civilian evacuation in armed conflict from a seven-dimension risk score and historical cases.

contribution.roleNote: Developed by Yago Rocha in collaboration with the Microsoft Ethical Tech CoLab.

narrative.problem: Planners deciding whether to evacuate civilians from a conflict zone need to weigh the cost of moving people now against the mounting cost of assisting those who stay, under uncertain threat, access, authorization and logistics conditions, with little calibrated evidence to hand.
narrative.decision: Frames the choice as a break-even between a one-time evacuation cost and cumulative daily in-zone assistance cost, and tags every cost parameter as Validated, Estimated or Unvalidated so the evidence behind each figure stays visible.
narrative.tradeoff: The headline break-even is driven by the least-evidenced parameters yet, as the peer review notes, is delivered as a single point with no uncertainty band; mortality is deliberately kept out of assistance costs to avoid implying a financial value on human life.
narrative.limitation: The mortality model is indicative, not predictive: calibrated on 16 of 31 historical cases with 7 of 16 within 2x, and level L4 cannot capture both urban sieges and precision enclave operations. The peer review recommends major revisions.
narrative.caveat: Not operational advice: cost figures are logistics estimates only and do not value human life. The free-tier backend can take up to a minute to wake, and saved scenarios reset when it restarts.

projects.title: The Human Choice: AI, Power & Dignity Field Guide
projects.summary: A source-grounded briefing and teaching package on AI, power and human dignity, with a static dashboard, course map, event briefs and interactive demos for classes, salons and policy discussions.

narrative.problem: Discussion of the AI transition often mixes dated scenarios, authors' claims and recommendations as if they were settled fact. The project asks how societies can remain the authors of the AI transition rather than merely its audience, starting from nine supplied sources.
narrative.decision: Labels every claim by type (observed fact, source claim, scenario, recommendation, synthesis or question) and anchors deliverables to primary sources, so the dated narratives of AI 2027 and AI 2040 are never presented as established facts.
narrative.tradeoff: Working from nine anchor sources and labeled claims keeps the analysis auditable but narrows its coverage, and the DAPPR synthesis is the project's own framework rather than one any single source claims.
narrative.limitation: A draft with no public reuse license yet; it rests on nine supplied sources retrieved on August 30, 2026, and its demos are teaching exercises with no reported evaluation.
narrative.caveat: DAPPR is this project's own interpretive framework. Scenario content is labeled as scenario, and the self-assessment demos are teaching exercises, not legal, compliance or human-rights reviews.

projects.title: Ethical AI Proxy
projects.summary: A lightweight CORS proxy that lets Ethical Tech CoLab GitHub Pages demos make live calls to the Claude API or GPU-hosted models without exposing API keys in browser code.

narrative.problem: GitHub Pages is static hosting: a demo there cannot hide API keys, because everything is visible in the browser, cannot make server-side API calls, and cannot get past CORS restrictions to reach the lab's own GPU server.
narrative.decision: A small server, run on the GPU server or any server, holds the API keys, allowlists GitHub Pages origins, rate-limits requests and forwards them to the Claude API or to one configured GPU inference server; a browser client helper offers ask, stream and GPU calls.
narrative.tradeoff: Keys never reach the browser, but every AI-enabled demo now depends on a separately operated server staying up, and the GPU route forwards only to the configured server, so it deliberately cannot act as a general relay.
narrative.limitation: The README covers setup, endpoints and security controls but reports no tests, load evaluation or deployment record; operators must supply their own process management (pm2 or systemd) and configuration.

projects.title: Evacuation Simulator
projects.summary: An interactive agent-based model that lets students and humanitarians explore how information spread and demographics shape community evacuation behavior.

contribution.roleNote: Developed by Melanie MacKew as masters research at the NYU Center for Global Affairs (2026), under the Ethical Tech CoLab.

narrative.problem: In humanitarian evacuations, who leaves and when depends on how information spreads and on household demographics: alerts must be confirmed, neighbours influence one another, and elders, young children, pregnant people and unaccompanied minors move more slowly.
narrative.decision: Households are modelled as family clusters whose hub waits for every member, and each member must confirm an alert before milling begins; every transition from unaware to done is probabilistic and depends on threat level, info clarity and household composition.
narrative.tradeoff: Because transitions are probabilistic, a single run shows little and results need multi-run comparison; some outcomes, such as cars equalising vulnerability, follow directly from the parameter table rather than emerging from the model.
narrative.limitation: The independent peer review recommends major revisions and notes that no empirical output is reported: not a single run, figure or distribution.
narrative.caveat: A research prototype for academic demonstration and teaching only. Outputs are illustrative and are not a substitute for operational planning, legal advice, or assessment by qualified humanitarian and IHL professionals.

projects.title: Evacuation Inform Index (EII)
projects.summary: A composite index and interactive world map that scores 104 INFORM Severity crises on the risk of evacuating against the risk of staying, for comparing crises at a strategic level.

contribution.roleNote: Summer 2026 Ethical Tech CoLab cohort project; Yorke advised.

narrative.problem: Comparing crises means weighing the danger of staying against the risk of leaving, yet INFORM publishes no coordinates, and whether the roads out are usable, the most decisive input to evacuation feasibility, is reported by no open global feed for conflict zones.
narrative.decision: Places every crisis at a curated location, labelled as a sub-national area, a reception area or a population-weighted country point, instead of offset country centroids that put about three quarters of points somewhere the crisis is not.
narrative.tradeoff: 65 crises remain country-level stand-ins, and six are flagged low-confidence because a more precise point could not be assigned without inventing one; road reports are pinned at the crisis, never at the blockage.
narrative.limitation: Weights are preliminary, pending AHP expert surveys; only monthly fatalities enter the conflict score, road status is keyword-derived from headlines, and the ratio is least informative for the severity-5 crises.
narrative.caveat: Not for advising anyone whether to leave, operational go/no-go, route selection or justifying a restriction on movement. One score per crisis, mostly country-level; the hosted site shows a frozen data snapshot.

projects.title: Exodus — Civilian Evacuation Risk Platform
projects.summary: A single FastAPI web platform for civilian-evacuation planning that unifies a crisis map, the ERCF scenario cost model and the CERAI risk assessment behind one backend and interface.

contribution.roleNote: Unifies Ethical Tech CoLab tools: EII, ERCF, CERAI and the route and behavioral simulators.

narrative.problem: Civilian-evacuation risk tools built separately, a crisis-information map, a scenario cost model and a risk anticipation index, each answer part of the question and run on their own backends, data sources and keys, so a planner has to move between them.
narrative.decision: Brings the three tools together as tabs of one FastAPI application, so all three share one backend, one design language and one set of API keys, with scenario storage in SQLite.
narrative.tradeoff: The platform carries copies of its component models that must be re-synced when their upstream repositories change, and its live features depend on several third-party services (INFORM/ACAPS, ACLED, Tavily, GDELT, Anthropic), with fallbacks when keys are missing.
narrative.limitation: The README documents no evaluation, tests or limitations of its own, and the CoLab's After the Corridor report lists Exodus as built and operational but not yet validated.
narrative.caveat: Country analysis is AI-generated (Claude, with a fallback), and live news and conflict data depend on third-party API keys; the platform is not validated for operational evacuation decisions.

projects.title: Felementum
projects.summary: An interactive 3D explorer for N-tier supply chain networks that follows materials from OEMs down to the mines, for spotting systemic suppliers and single-country dependencies.

narrative.problem: Supply chains run many tiers deep, from finished products through module integrators, component makers and refiners to extraction sites, so systemic suppliers, single-country dependencies and hidden concentration risk are hard to see from any single tier.
narrative.decision: Runs entirely in the browser as a static site on seeded synthetic data, with an optional data assistant that works locally or with the visitor's own AI provider key, held only in browser memory.
narrative.tradeoff: No real supplier data is shown, so concentration and exposure figures demonstrate the method rather than describe any company, and larger datasets must be downloaded to the browser (about 6 MB for the stress set).
narrative.limitation: Company names and supplier relationships are fictional and mine capacities approximate; the 68 Playwright checks test the interface, and no validation of the risk measures against real supply chains is reported.
narrative.caveat: Synthetic data: company names and supplier relationships are fictional. Mine sites are real public locations, but their capacities are approximate and for illustration only; nothing describes any real company's supply chain.

projects.title: Forced Labor Structural Risk Index (FLSRI)
projects.summary: A country-level index, scored 0–1, of the structural conditions under which forced labor becomes more likely, published as an interactive site with uncertainty bands for researchers and policymakers.

contribution.roleNote: Developed under the Ethical Tech CoLab at the NYU Center for Global Affairs as part of masters research (2026).

narrative.problem: Forced labor is largely hidden, so a country index cannot count or estimate cases. What can be compared are the structural conditions that make recruitment and exploitation more likely, and those must be measured transparently, with thin data and uncertainty stated rather than hidden.
narrative.decision: The headline score is the geometric mean of Recruitment × Exploitation, built from indicators standardized against fixed literature-based anchors; a coverage floor leaves thin-data countries unscored rather than imputed, and each score carries a 90% rank band from 10,000 seeded Monte Carlo re-scorings.
narrative.tradeoff: The geometric mean penalizes imbalance and the no-imputation rule avoids misleading values, but 11 of about 195 countries go unscored, Monetization is computed yet excluded from the composite, and the wide bands leave mid-table ranks hard to read.
narrative.limitation: It reads origin-side risk and under-reads destination and sponsorship systems such as kafala, so several Gulf destination states score low; validation covers the structure, not individual scores, and there is no clean external prevalence benchmark. Peer review recommended major revisions.
narrative.caveat: Scores estimate structural conditions, not prevalence. Read them in tiers with their uncertainty bands, not as exact ranks, legal findings about any state or compliance assessments of any enterprise.

projects.title: Fraternity
projects.summary: Comparative situation research across protracted refugee and displacement crises, building a sourced evidence base to find high-leverage intervention opportunities before narrowing to one.

contribution.roleNote: NYU student independent study for the fall 2026 semester.

narrative.problem: Protracted refugee and displacement crises differ in their legal and policy settings, funding, disaster risk and protection pathways. Finding a lever that is high-leverage, tractable and neglected needs comparable, sourced situation data across several sites, not one case studied in isolation.
narrative.decision: Breadth before depth: one reusable four-pathway method is applied across camps, with one case file per crisis following the same structure so cases can be compared side by side before going deep on any single opportunity.
narrative.tradeoff: Prioritising breadth defers deep work on any one site until a cross-case comparison surfaces an opportunity, and figures that diverge across sources are kept unreconciled, so each must be checked by date before it is used comparatively.
narrative.limitation: Since 19 October 2026 the work has shifted to NameBridge, cross-border name intelligence for missing-person search, which is a research prototype: offline, synthetic data only, no live case decisions. The situation research is kept for reference only.

projects.title: GBV Patterns
projects.summary: An advocacy and research platform on femicide and gender-based violence, built with the Coalition Against Trafficking in Women, making the case for New York to become the first US state to name femicide in law.

contribution.roleNote: Built by the Ethical Tech CoLab at NYU with the Coalition Against Trafficking in Women (CATW); first shown at the Ethical Tech Summit, 20 November 2026.

narrative.problem: About three dozen countries define femicide in their criminal codes and no US state does. New York counts domestic violence homicides by borough and relationship, but a woman killed by a buyer, a pimp or a trafficker has no category to be counted in.
narrative.decision: Shows the Women Count USA databases only through their author's own published share links, rather than aggregating them, and keeps raw exports containing names, photos and narratives out of the repository.
narrative.tradeoff: Case-level patterns cannot be charted on the site until Dawn Wilcox and CATW agree in writing; until then visitors log counts by hand with a tally tool.
narrative.limitation: The number of femicides in the sex trade is unknown, not zero; county-level enforcement counts are not published, and the Progress page and BACKLOG.md list what is not yet built or researched.
narrative.caveat: Describes femicide, rape and trafficking, including real cases. Every figure links to its source; figures quoted from secondary summaries are flagged.

projects.title: ETC Grant Valuator
projects.summary: An AI-assisted grant valuation and pipeline tool for the Ethical Tech CoLab that scores funding prospects against the lab's mission and tracks applications from prospect through award and reporting.

contribution.roleNote: Ethical Tech CoLab internal tool with an accompanying research paper and peer review.

narrative.problem: A small research lab has to find grant opportunities, judge which fit its mission and are worth the effort, write to each funder's review criteria, and keep track of deadlines, applications, awards and reporting across a pipeline.
narrative.decision: Claude (claude-opus-4-8) returns per-criterion scores, win probability, red flags and a pursue / consider / pass recommendation, but the fit score is computed in code as the weighted average of the five criterion scores using fixed weights in mission.ts.
narrative.tradeoff: Win probability, which drives expected value, remains the model's judgement and nothing calibrates it yet; the peer review found two-thirds of the pipeline's expected value rests on a single unvalidated estimate.
narrative.limitation: A stability check (re-scoring the same grants) and the calibration loop are still open. Grants live in a committed JSON file that is not safe for concurrent writes or multi-user use, and there is no authentication yet.
narrative.caveat: The GitHub Pages link is a static overview; the full tool needs a Node server and an Anthropic API key. Fit scores and win probabilities are AI judgements, not calibrated predictions.

projects.title: Evacuation Readiness & Uncertainty Simulator
projects.summary: A browser-based research instrument that models how uncertain field intelligence degrades decisions about where to evacuate civilians in armed conflict, built for doctoral research on civilian protection.

contribution.roleNote: Doctoral research by India Clarke under the Ethical Tech CoLab at the NYU Center for Global Affairs.

narrative.problem: When humanitarian organisations decide where to move civilians fleeing conflict, they choose among destinations they do not fully understand: security reports may be stale, authority consent assumed and host-community willingness never asked. Decision quality can collapse while nothing on the ground has changed.
narrative.decision: Treats Security, Authority consent and Willingness as non-substitutable gatekeepers that can cap readiness at 20%, and distinguishes an unassessed factor (Unknown) from a host community's confirmed refusal (Unwilling).
narrative.tradeoff: Uncertainty enters through one auditable formula, so the downward sensitivity curve is a built-in assumption made explicit rather than an independent finding, and hard caps make a strong site with one blocked gatekeeper score like a weak one.
narrative.limitation: A conceptual demonstration on synthetic data: outputs need empirical calibration, the 40% success threshold is an unsourced internal assumption, and the information-value ranking is not statistically resolvable at its default 100 runs.
narrative.caveat: All destinations and evacuee groups are synthetic and generated from a seed. This is a research and teaching demonstration, not an operational decision-support system, and its outputs are uncalibrated.

projects.title: Manhattan Bridge Digital Twin
projects.summary: A source-governed, part-addressable digital twin of the Manhattan Bridge for browser rendering and HO-scale study, in which every dimension traces to a registered source with a confidence grade.

narrative.problem: No existing 3D model of the Manhattan Bridge is authoritative, and there is no public measured drawing of it — the HAER survey contains photographs and no drawings — so a detailed model easily ends up inventing dimensions it cannot source.
narrative.decision: Official dimensions and archival drawings in GEOMETRY-CONTROL.md are the control geometry: scripts parse it and carry no numbers of their own, anything without a registered source is tagged confidence D, and geometry provenance is drawn as solid, dashed and dotted outlines so uncertainty is visible by default.
narrative.tradeoff: Refusing to invent dimensions keeps the model honest, but 66 of 103 parts remain grade D and 14 of 78 control values are placeholders; photographs can grade materials but cannot promote a dimension above D without scale control.
narrative.limitation: The remaining placeholders wait on NYC DOT and MTA record drawings that are not public, for which a FOIL request is prepared; none of the 253 audit photographs has been reviewed yet, and CI skips schema validation of the published contract documents.
narrative.caveat: Most parts are inferred or placeholder geometry. Switching off inferred and assumed parts in the viewer leaves the towers, anchorages and station markers — the whole of what the model can be said to document.

projects.title: Silencing the Span
projects.summary: An open research programme that defines the subway rail-noise problem from the Manhattan Bridge in DUMBO, Brooklyn, as the evidence a design-build intervention would need before procurement.

narrative.problem: B, D, N and Q trains cross the Manhattan Bridge roughly every 76 seconds, about 20 hours a day, and the MTA measured 87.50 dB(A) Leq at the Brooklyn Bridge Park dog run. Twenty-one years of measurement have produced no mitigation: the state rapid-transit noise code leaves the level for elevated structures "to be established", and NYC 311 has no category for rail noise.
narrative.decision: It is deliberately a problem definition, not a design: every citation carries a verification state, each document gets an adversarial red-team pass, and withdrawn claims are quoted in place rather than quietly deleted.
narrative.tradeoff: No option in any document is recommended for procurement, and most findings stay hedged until methods that need records requests, field measurement or surveys are actually carried out.
narrative.limitation: No calibrated acoustic measurement has been taken and no survey has been made; of the 48 methods specified, six have been executed and one partially. None of the documents is peer-reviewed.
narrative.caveat: The acoustic demonstration uses an assumed spectrum, the agent model uses invented itineraries, and the 3D wireframe is inferred geometry rather than a survey.

projects.title: Humanitarian Corridors Under Siege: Mariupol 2022
projects.summary: A retrospective decision-support prototype that scores daily danger and evacuation feasibility for civilians during the 2022 siege of Mariupol, anchored in international humanitarian law.

contribution.roleNote: Ethical Tech CoLab fork of ChristineLumen/mariupol-evacuation-model; Yorke advised.

narrative.problem: During the siege of Mariupol, 5 March – 20 May 2022, civilians faced daily danger from hostilities, deprivation and infrastructure destruction, while the negotiated evacuation mechanism envisaged by GC IV art. 17 arrived only on 30 April.
narrative.decision: Combines six normalised severity components with a generalised power mean (p = 6, weakest-link), so the worst component drives the daily score instead of being averaged away, and pairs it with a satellite-based feasibility axis.
narrative.tradeoff: The exponent, normalisation bounds and phase thresholds are documented conventions, and the sensitivity analysis shows two results, 'violence never dominates' and the Critical phase, do not survive alternative settings.
narrative.limitation: Retrospective and only partially validated against observed displacement; event reporting degrades inside the besieged city as severity peaks, and district demographics in the feasibility axis are author's estimates.
narrative.caveat: Retrospective research prototype, not operational guidance. Front lines and damage zones are approximate, and the same data fusion that prioritises evacuation could support targeting.

projects.title: Neocloud Supply OS
projects.summary: An agent-first operating system concept for a neocloud's supply chain, from GPU sourcing and data center build to logistics and third-party risk, with a static simulation and negotiation demo.

contribution.roleNote: Risk-provider MCP patterns credited to the supplier-risk playbook in isislcn/Hazard-and-Suppliers; simulation and negotiation concepts from CoLab projects.

narrative.problem: A neocloud turning signed customer demand into powered, revenue-earning GPU capacity has to coordinate chips, hardware, data center construction, logistics, asset lifecycle and third-party risk, typically across a portfolio of about 140 separate legacy applications.
narrative.decision: The design names no third-party risk provider: every risk call goes through eleven canonical capabilities behind a RISK_PROVIDER variable, and a registry maps each capability to a provider's native MCP tool or API call.
narrative.tradeoff: Provider function names do not converge (only get_entity matches exactly), so each provider needs a hand-built mapping that records how every native name is known, and the standard is fixed at the capability level rather than the tool level.
narrative.limitation: The concept is signed off but the specification awaits human review with 33 open questions, 11 of them blocking. There is no production code; the economic estimates in the simulation need operational calibration before use in a business case.
narrative.caveat: All data on the site is simulated: suppliers, counterparties and risk-provider signals are fictional and no provider is called. Brand themes are approximations, not affiliated with or endorsed by any company.

projects.title: PageTurn Book V3
projects.summary: A framework-neutral semantic book reader and publication library that keeps text as native HTML while adding page-turn geometry, for publishing scholarly books and reports on the web.

narrative.problem: Fixed-page book viewers rasterize publication text, which costs native, accessible and searchable HTML and durable links to individual passages. Scholarly publications need a reader that still turns like a book while keeping text semantic and citable.
narrative.decision: Publications are compiled from metadata and Markdown into immutable manifests and directly readable chapter HTML; the reader loads only a bounded current and adjacent chapter window and projects StPageFlip-derived page-turn geometry onto accessible semantic page faces.
narrative.tradeoff: Keeping text as live HTML preserves accessibility, search and durable source anchors, but every book must go through the publication compiler, and the older V2 reader and V1 fixed-page viewer are kept as compatibility paths that still need testing.
narrative.limitation: Public npm registry publication is blocked until the project license is approved, so consumers must build and install a tarball; quote sharing, share composing and external previews stay off unless the host supplies an explicit policy.

projects.title: Plumb
projects.summary: A browser-based tool for architectural and preservation work that produces measured, verifiable photographs of historic buildings and bridges, with a calibrated grid and ruler and C2PA provenance.

narrative.problem: Architectural and preservation work needs photographs that are evidence, not illustrations: images you can measure from, whose location, creator, date and lineage can be verified. The HABS/HAER/HALS documentation standards already require a scale in the photograph.
narrative.decision: C2PA is the provenance backbone: raw captures are signed at ingest and every derivative names its parents as C2PA ingredients, while authoritative measurement happens in server-side post-processing that can be re-run later on the same immutable bytes.
narrative.tradeoff: As a browser app it cannot reach on-device keystore signing, the only route to C2PA Assurance Level 2, so that is deferred; Android Chrome is the primary platform and iOS Safari gets an honestly labelled reduced feature set.
narrative.limitation: It is not survey-grade: achievable accuracy is roughly USIBD LOA20–LOA10 for marker-calibrated single images, measurements are exact only on the calibrated plane, and it does not replace a total station, laser scan or licensed survey.
narrative.caveat: Needs a phone camera over HTTPS; Android Chrome gets the full feature set. Measurement stays disabled until the grid is calibrated, and results are not a licensed survey.

projects.title: Arts & Artifacts — Provenance Intelligence
projects.summary: A research prototype that looks up an artwork's ownership history across free public sources and emits a provenance passport with a confidence score computed by a fixed algorithm, not by the AI.

contribution.roleNote: Developed under the Ethical Tech CoLab at the NYU Center for Global Affairs as part of masters research (2026).

narrative.problem: An object with an unexplained break in its ownership history may have been stolen, looted in war or illegally excavated, but the records are scattered across museum accession files, auction catalogues, police reports and heir claims that rarely speak to one another.
narrative.decision: Gemini identifies images and assembles the timeline from retrieved facts, but the confidence score is computed entirely in server.js by fixed, published deductions, and general-knowledge entries are labelled and never marked verified.
narrative.tradeoff: Fixed rules keep the score transparent but blunt: a well-documented history containing a wartime seizure and an obscure object with no history can both score very low, and the number alone does not distinguish them.
narrative.limitation: The weights are the developer's judgment, not derived from a study, expert panel or validation against known cases; nothing checks the model-assembled timeline against retrieved material; searches are simple text matches over a Western-weighted source list.
narrative.caveat: For academic demonstration only: results are indicative, not a clearance or certificate of title. It searches the public web pages of INTERPOL, the Art Loss Register and others, not their restricted databases.

projects.title: Quest Payments
projects.summary: A design for event ticketing in which attendees lower their ticket price by completing verifiable actions, with settlement in USDC stablecoins over the x402 protocol, for event organizers.

narrative.problem: A flat ticket price does nothing to reward the actions that help an event succeed, such as sharing it, referring friends, checking in on time or giving feedback, and settling many small conditional discounts through card networks means expiring authorizations or non-recoverable refund fees.
narrative.decision: Separates a familiar card checkout on the front end from back-end settlement in USDC via Coinbase's x402 protocol on low-cost L2 networks (Base, Arbitrum), capturing only the net amount once incentive actions resolve.
narrative.tradeoff: Auth-then-capture is limited by card authorizations that expire in 2 to 7 days, charge-then-refund loses processing fees, and the most cost-efficient option, stablecoin escrow, requires crypto-native users or an on-ramp.
narrative.limitation: Early design and research phase: no live checkout or on-chain settlement exists, and the license is still to be decided. The published site explains the concept and offers a builder for configuring incentive campaigns.
narrative.caveat: Early design and research phase. The site takes no payments: the quest builder only configures and exports incentive definitions, and its demo quests are examples.

projects.title: Race Condition — Evacuation Twin
projects.summary: A fork of the Race Condition multi-agent marathon simulation, repurposed as a location-swappable civilian evacuation twin for planning and education, with a DTSF twin backend and browser-run city scenarios.

contribution.roleNote: Modifies Race Condition (GoogleCloudPlatform/race-condition) by Casey West and the Race Condition team at Google; derivative work under Apache 2.0.

narrative.problem: Upstream Race Condition models thousands of autonomous agents moving along a route through a real 3D city. Civilian evacuation is structurally the same problem — many people, imperfect information, shared routes, bottlenecks, stopping points and a clock — but needs location-specific scenarios grounded in open data rather than a marathon.
narrative.decision: Each scenario is opt-in through a ?scenario=<id> URL parameter and a pure-data pack (building footprints, routes, POIs, damage) drawn by a GLB-less schematic renderer, so the upstream Vegas marathon stays render-identical and the static build runs on GitHub Pages with no backend or API keys.
narrative.tradeoff: Pure-data scenarios run offline at no cost, but they are rendered schematically and are not yet driven by the live multi-agent engine: the Go gateway and ADK agents still run the Vegas marathon, and the DTSF twin replays a deterministic trajectory instead of the realtime WebSocket stream.
narrative.limitation: Evacuation behaviour in the backend is largely an RFC: scenarios are not wired into the live engine, cohort movement and hazard-aware routing are parameters rather than agent behaviour, the DTSF twin control plane is open work, building heights are hashed, and the NYC Marathon route is about 88% of the official distance.
narrative.caveat: Planning and education exercise over open and synthetic data: zones, exits, corridors and demographics are illustrative and building heights are hashed. Not operational; it must not be used to locate or interdict people.

projects.title: Resilience Atlas
projects.summary: An interactive browser guide to supply chain resilience and reverse stress testing for learners and researchers, with a teaching brief, a concept atlas, a synthetic reverse stress lab and a source library.

narrative.problem: A supplier that is safe on its own does not make a resilient network: hidden risk can sit in a combination of dependencies, and forward scenario tests only check the disruptions someone thought to imagine.
narrative.decision: Starts from an outcome that must not fail and works backward to the disruptions that could cause it, taught entirely in the browser with no external AI, tracking or uploads, on an anonymised High Tech, SI and ISV scenario.
narrative.tradeoff: The reverse stress lab is a synthetic single-layer normal-model example, so its outputs illustrate the method rather than giving calibrated risk scores, and learner notes stay in one browser without syncing.
narrative.limitation: Teaching material, not a validated operational tool or established standard; the roadmap to reproduce methods, build benchmarks and run a bounded shadow-mode pilot is proposed, not implemented.
narrative.caveat: The scenario is illustrative, not a confirmed partnership or product capability, and the lab's outputs are not forecasts or calibrated risk scores.

projects.title: Sovereign Agent Trust Mesh (SATM)
projects.summary: A prototype trust fabric that lets AI agents in different organizations verify who owns an agent, what authority it holds and what it has done, by joining Google SAM with ERC-8004 and ERC-8226 registries.

narrative.problem: AI agents can already talk to each other and invoke tools, but they cannot trust each other across organizational boundaries without a pre-existing relationship. Google SAM has no global reputation or verifiable mandates, ERC-8004 has no transport, ERC-8226 has neither, and nothing binds a libp2p PeerID to an on-chain agentId.
narrative.decision: An Agent Mesh Binding: one canonical document signed twice, by the node's libp2p host key and by the agent's ERC-8004 agentWallet via EIP-712, so on-chain identity can gate mesh traffic; SAM is integrated unforked through documented HTTP and YAML seams.
narrative.tradeoff: The chain is the source of truth and the mesh only caches it, so revocation lands at the next reconcile sweep, non-asset decisions may proceed within bounded, logged staleness windows, and an RPC outage revokes nothing rather than everything.
narrative.limitation: Phase 2 is 11 of 14 tasks done. Outbound sidecar authorization returns 501 pending the Phase 3 trust plane; the enrollment gate, CLI, indexer, mandates and agents are not started; the devnet compose has not been run; ERC-8226 is a draft EIP implemented from its text.

images.caption: The missing joint: network identity and on-chain identity are not bound, so on-chain trust cannot gate mesh traffic. SATM's binding closes that gap.

projects.title: teardown
projects.summary: A Claude Code skill that builds any machine as an offline 3D simulator you can take apart, extended here with a BOM-driven Lenovo AI rack teardown that highlights parts named by external risk signals.

contribution.roleNote: Extends elvarofficial/teardown.

narrative.problem: Seeing how a machine works, or which physical part a component or supplier risk signal affects, usually means reading diagrams, spec sheets and bills of materials separately instead of inspecting the parts in context.
narrative.decision: Has Claude build each machine as one offline HTML page of procedural Three.js geometry; the Lenovo rack reads every part, count, dimension and wattage from a swappable BOM file and accepts risk signals by URL, postMessage or a JavaScript API.
narrative.tradeoff: Procedural geometry is not vendor CAD, so dimensions and wattages are illustrative, and different mechanical architectures need new geometry rather than a same-shape SKU swap.
narrative.limitation: Rack presets are illustrative examples, not certified order BOMs; the default risk signals are fictional, and the fan switch animates rotors without simulating airflow, cooling or electrical state.
narrative.caveat: Not affiliated with or endorsed by Lenovo, NVIDIA or AMD. Dimensions, specifications and wattages are illustrative, and the default risk signals are fictional demo data, not findings about any real product or supplier.

projects.title: Turnstone
projects.summary: A browser tool for photographing cultural objects from every side so the resulting 3D record states how good it is and what it may be relied on for, with signed provenance from photographs to mesh.

contribution.roleNote: Provides the metric extractors and mobile client that the Ethical-Tech-CoLab/DPA capture rubric states it lacks.

narrative.problem: A 3D model of a statue, vessel or mask is only worth something afterwards if it says how good it is. DPA defines a ten-dimension capture rubric but states it has no metric extractors and no mobile client, and photogrammetry captures often skip coverage underneath and around an object.
narrative.decision: The rubric is data, with every threshold in one file; live extractors compute sharpness, exposure, overlap, coverage and scale from actual pixels, and the record's class is the worst dimension, never the average. Records bind photographs to the mesh with Ed25519 signatures and mandatory attests / doesNotAttest fields.
narrative.tradeoff: Worst-dimension scoring always names the one thing to fix, but a single weak dimension caps the whole record, and device metadata cannot be scored live, so live classes stay provisional until the final assessment.
narrative.limitation: Surface completeness is only an estimate (open question OQ-1), device metadata is deferred, the reconstruction container is unbuilt, and the IIIF 3D export follows a draft. A capture says nothing about lawful ownership and is deliberately not an input to provenance confidence.
narrative.caveat: Browser storage is not an archive: photographs live in IndexedDB until exported and can be evicted. A flawless capture is not a claim of lawful ownership.

projects.title: usage-calc
projects.summary: A command-line tool that reads the GitHub Copilot CLI's local request ledger and publishes what an AI-assisted project cost in money, tokens, model time and human time as one self-contained page.

narrative.problem: Almost every public claim about what AI-assisted work costs rests on an invented denominator: a remembered number of hours, a guessed number of requests, a rate nobody published.
narrative.decision: It reads the per-request SQLite ledger the Copilot CLI writes as it works, with the model, token counts, duration and billed price, and refuses to print a total it cannot reconcile; the output is a single HTML page with no CDN, build step or server.
narrative.tradeoff: The ledger is per machine, so a dashboard built on one laptop is a floor, not a total: other machines must be exported and merged by hand, and a machine nobody remembers stays invisible.
narrative.limitation: The dollar figure is a list-price equivalent, not a bill; person time is an inferred residual that cannot distinguish thinking from lunch; the energy panel is an estimate whose bracket spans a factor of 24; and nothing measures whether the output was worth having.

projects.title: VANGO — Art Passport
projects.summary: A mobile-style digital passport in which art visitors collect a stamp for each artwork they see by scanning a QR code or entering its code; a student research prototype on audience engagement.

contribution.roleNote: Developed by Melanie MacKew as masters research at the NYU Center for Global Affairs (2026), under the Ethical Tech CoLab; Yorke advised.

narrative.problem: Most people who visit a museum, a biennale or a small studio exhibition leave with nothing to show for it, and for the institution the encounter is equally invisible.
narrative.decision: Borrows the travel passport: a stamp records only that a person saw a particular work on a particular day, not ownership, value or authenticity, and in guest mode nothing leaves the visitor's phone.
narrative.tradeoff: A public code proves nothing about presence: anyone holding it can collect the stamp from anywhere. Signed stamp tokens are verified server-side, but bare codes are still accepted because the printed QR codes encode them.
narrative.limitation: Seven catalogue works, five of them fictional; never placed in a real exhibition or tested with visitors, and the published demo cannot sign anyone in because its server address points to a local machine.
narrative.caveat: Academic demonstration only: five of the seven artworks are fictional, account sign-in does not work on the public demo, and a stamp is not evidence of attendance, ownership or lawful origin.

projects.title: Shall We Play a Game?
projects.summary: A browser terminal thriller inspired by WarGames (1983) in which players face a polite, literal AI in scripted or live language-model mode, built as a teaching tool on autonomous AI agents.

contribution.roleNote: The accompanying paper, The Only Winning Move, was prepared by Carolina Morón as masters research at the NYU Center for Global Affairs.

narrative.problem: Learners rarely get to watch a language model behave as an autonomous agent under pressure, or see the line between deterministic rules and emergent model behavior. WarGames' machine is courteous, literal and relentless rather than malicious, which makes it a frame for exactly that lesson.
narrative.decision: The model never owns state or rules: in Live AI mode it must return a reply, a DEFCON change and an optional ending under a strict JSON contract, and deterministic code validates and decides; chess legality and tic-tac-toe never use a model at all.
narrative.tradeoff: Resolution still waits on the model to declare an ending: in the Monte Carlo study, 16–25% of real-model games hit the 12-turn cap and were force-ended, and the recommended fix is for the engine to drive resolution.
narrative.limitation: The film name set is for prototyping only. A guided educational lesson and debrief, an original public-release name set and a stable proxy endpoint are open roadmap items; Live AI currently reaches the self-hosted proxy through an ephemeral tunnel.
narrative.caveat: In Live AI mode the machine's lines are generated by a language model and marked ◆; if the AI proxy is unreachable the game falls back to Scripted mode. The scenario is fictional.

projects.title: webpage-note
projects.summary: A small opt-in JavaScript widget that lets website owners and reviewers attach notes to page elements and turn them into prefilled GitHub issues for follow-up.

narrative.problem: Website owners and reviewers lack a common way to leave feedback tied to the exact element they mean: a feedback issue form can ask for a URL and a screenshot, but it cannot attach a comment to an individual part of the page.
narrative.decision: Ships as one dependency-free script, off unless configured, that keeps notes locally and opens a prefilled GitHub issue with the comment, page URL, CSS selector and captured text, with no GitHub token and no automatic submission.
narrative.tradeoff: Reviewers must review and submit each issue themselves and need permission to create issues; submitted issues are not synced back onto the page, and selectors can go stale when the page structure changes.
narrative.limitation: There is no test runner or build tooling, so validation is a syntax check plus manual browser testing; notes inside iframes or shadow DOM are not supported, and saves from multiple tabs overwrite each other.

projects.title: Ethical Tech CoLab Website
projects.summary: The public website of the NYU Center for Global Affairs × Microsoft Research Ethical Tech CoLab, presenting its cohorts, research projects, live demos, publications, team and newsletter.

narrative.problem: The CoLab's projects move from research question to fielded prototype within a semester-long cohort, leaving many separate repositories, demos and reports. Visitors need one public place to find the cohorts, research projects, live demos, publications, newsletter and team.
narrative.decision: A Next.js App Router site keeps most general site data in one content module (src/content/site.ts), with publication reports and newsletter metadata in their own modules, so content is edited at its source rather than in presentation components; a generated static-site snapshot is committed alongside the source.
narrative.tradeoff: Typed content modules keep names, projects and links consistent across pages, but every content change is a code edit and rebuild rather than a CMS entry, which is why the repository carries a content guide, a contribution workflow and recommended repository controls.
narrative.limitation: The About route is hidden and returns 404, team headshots are added by hand, and open content work is tracked in BACKLOG.md and UPDATES-NEEDED.md; the README documents no automated content or accessibility evaluation.

projects.title: What Is Ethical AI?
projects.summary: The Ethical Tech CoLab's foundational paper, tracing ethics from early civilizations through international relations and human rights law to responsible and humanitarian AI.

contribution.roleNote: Master's research (M.S. in Global Affairs) at the NYU Center for Global Affairs, published by the Ethical Tech CoLab in collaboration with Microsoft.

narrative.problem: AI ethics guidance has multiplied, with 84 guidelines mapped converging on five principles but diverging on how to apply them, while 118 countries, overwhelmingly in the Global South, are party to none of the major AI governance initiatives the UN surveyed.
narrative.decision: The paper's answer is institutional rather than technical: ethical AI is not a product feature but AI whose entire lifecycle stays accountable to ethical deliberation, to human rights as a floor, to do no harm, and to the participation of those it affects.
narrative.tradeoff: An institutional framing gives no technical test a system can pass; it places responsibility on the institutions that govern AI, so the argument cannot certify any particular system as ethical in itself.
narrative.limitation: It is a conceptual paper that reports no original evaluation. The designed PDF still carries two errors fixed in the web text, and the references carry no URLs or DOIs, so citations were not link-checked.

projects.title: Williamsburg Bridge — source-governed digital twin
projects.summary: A browser 3D model of the Williamsburg Bridge in which every part carries its provenance, so a reader can ask of any surface how it is known and get a real answer, including 'we do not'.

narrative.problem: The national record for the Williamsburg Bridge, HAER NY-128, contains no measured drawings and one sentence of dimensions, so any 3D model of it either guesses or has to say where its evidence runs out.
narrative.decision: No dimension may exist in the model without a registered source and an explicit confidence grade; geometry provenance is derived in the build, and the published site deploys only if the traceability and regression test suites pass.
narrative.tradeoff: Almost everything is inferred, so turning off INFERRED in the viewer makes the bridge disappear, and unknowns such as the side-span length stay deliberately round placeholders instead of plausible guesses.
narrative.limitation: Milestone 1 only: no part is measured, 32 of 57 parts are graded D, 11 questions are open with 14 registered source conflicts, and the sourced approaches end about 22 m above mean high water because the sources do not close.
narrative.caveat: A schematic, not a survey: inferred parts render dashed, dimensions are withheld where provenance is not documented, and the HAER photographs are reference imagery only.
